item.title: Major Digital Bank In Paraguay Collapses With Half of Population's Savings
item.author: BeauHD
item.content:encoded:
Paraguayan President Santiago Pena resigned Thursday amid mass protests and impeachment threats following the collapse of Ueno Bank, a major digital lender with close ties to his administration and more than 60% of the country's adults as customers. Regulators seized the bank after uncovering risky insider lending and accounting irregularities that left its capital below legal requirements, locking millions of customers out of their savings. The Associated Press reports: Soon after winning its banking license in 2023, Ueno seemed to be everywhere in Paraguay. The digital lender, a rebranded version of a decades-old finance company, lured customers with generous cash-back offers on groceries, grew to more than 70 locations, sponsored Paraguay's national soccer team and plastered its name on the country's main stadium. Government money poured into Ueno's coffers under Pena. He also appointed Carlos Carvallo, president of Financiera Ueno, the predecessor to Ueno Bank, to run the central bank, the agency charged with supervising the digital lender. As of last month, Ueno reported holding roughly $800 million in public deposits, about a quarter of its total, including money from the state pension and health fund and the operators of Paraguay's giant hydroelectric dams.
Even as retirees' savings and other public money piled up at Ueno, worries were escalating inside the central bank. In June, its inspectors found a pattern of risky lending to insiders, reported ABC Color, a leading Paraguayan newspaper. Ueno had extended large sums to companies tied to its owners, beyond what the law allows and without enough collateral to cover the debts if they went bad. On a single day in September 2025, nearly $39 million had gone to three such companies. Pena repeatedly brushed off the warnings. As recently as last month, he defended Ueno and the central bank's oversight, dismissing the concerns as a smear campaign that was spooking the public.
But on Monday, it all came crashing down. Regulators investigating Ueno's loans to companies linked to its owners found poorly documented lending, the central bank said, as well as expenses the bank had wrongly counted as assets. Once the books were corrected, Ueno's capital, the cushion banks must keep to absorb losses, fell to less than half the legal minimum. The central bank seized the lender Tuesday and announced plans to move customers' accounts, along with whatever assets still hold value, to other banks before liquidating what's left. Ueno's app, cards and transfers went dark and its branches locked their doors, leaving desperate depositors lined up outside with no way to cash out their savings. On Wednesday, a rush to open new accounts elsewhere crashed other banks' mobile apps, fueling public panic. Officials say they had begun repaying depositors and opening accounts at other banks for the roughly 280,000 customers who had banked exclusively with Ueno.
"The banking system is sound," insisted Pedro Acosta Bernal, appointed interim central bank president Wednesday after Carvallo resigned at Pena's request.
Meanwhile, eight senior Ueno executives have been detained, including founder Miguel Vazquez and bank President Juan Manuel Gustale. "Prosecutors also charged 27 bank officials and business associates with offenses including breach of trust and attempted fraud," reports the AP.

item.title: Microsoft's Imagine Cup 'Evolves' From Student Competition To AI Startup Contest
item.author: BeauHD
item.content:encoded:
theodp writes: That Was Then: The Imagine Cup competition, Microsoft explained in a 2003 press release, "seeks to provide students [aged 16-and-up] around the world with resources to use technology and Web services to solve everyday problems [...] Imagine Cup is about empowering students to apply their creativity and knowledge toward making the world a more-connected place."
This Is Now: "Building is Hard. Selling is Harder." begins the "Why Imagine Cup?" promo video for the 2027 Imagine Cup competition, which is pivoting to an AI startup-first focus in recognition that "A new era for founders is here." "Since 2003, Imagine Cup has empowered emerging innovators to turn ambitious ideas into real-world solutions with Microsoft technology," Microsoft writes of the Imagine Cup Evolution. "Now part of Microsoft for Startups, Imagine Cup enters its next chapter in 2027, opening the competition to eligible early-stage startups and founders everywhere."
An Eligibility FAQ drives home the point that Imagine Cup is no longer a student-only competition: "Imagine Cup 2027 welcomes eligible early-stage startups across seven categories; founders do not need to be students." And if you think making high school students compete against seasoned full-time employees of startup companies seems a tad unfair, Microsoft advises: "Eligible student-led startups are encouraged to enter the Student Startup category but may choose an industry category instead." The #1 overall startup will win a $250,000 cash award and $1,000,000 in startup credits. However, Student Startup category entrants are ineligible for the open category prizes (where the 2nd-place winner gets $50,000 cash and $350,000 in credits, while 3rd place is good for $25,000 and $350,000 in credits); they will instead compete for a single prize of $25,000 cash and $250,000 in credits. The Official Rules (PDF) note that all startups must have a valid Azure Subscription ID and a Microsoft for Startups account.

item.title: Republicans Learn X Is the Echo Chamber
item.author: Matthew Gault
item.content:encoded: There's a BlazeTV YouTube video whose thumbnail shows the presenter with his arms around Anakin Skywalker and a gender-flipped Draco Malfoy called Malfoid. “Total Chud Victory?” It says. The video's title: “Young Right is Reclaiming Culture and Liberals Are Mad About it.”BlazeTV posted the video on November 2, the day before Democrats swept the midterms and started a political realignment in America so overwhelming that Republicans lost control of all the most powerful state positions in Texas.The video is a profound misreading of the political and cultural moment. It reminded me of stories of the Bolsheviks seizing the Winter Palace to discover tarot card playing courtiers who had no idea a revolution was happening in the streets.The American version was watching defense contractor Palmer Lucky dress up like Harry Potter on Halloween while standing . And it was Elon Musk — who spent roughly half a billion on the election only to see his chosen candidates fail — posting an AI generated picture of Anakin Skywalker sitting at the head of a happy fascist Star Wars family two days before the midterms.The online right has dominated American culture for a decade, or at least has dominated political narratives picked up by the mainstream media. Its memes and conspiracies drove news cycles. At first, the right’s memes filtered from random people on obscure Discord channels to Reddit’s r/the_donald or 4chan to Trump’s Twitter feed. More recently they’ve come from AI slop farms, from Musk, or from the administration itself. Powered by a well-funded media and podcast ecosystem, Fox News (and a propensity for shamelessness) its comedians, podcasters, and pundits became powerful celebrities and influencers, at least within Elon Musk’s X. This insular, often inscrutable world has given us Ben Shapiro, Nick Fuentes, Gamergate influencers, the streamer Asmongold, and a revolving door of characters who have shuffled interchangeably between Twitterverse celebritydom and actual government; Kash Patel, DataRepublican, Laura Loomer, Pete Hegseth, RFK Jr., Dan Bongino, the list goes on. It has been said many times that “Twitter is not real life,” and that posting too much anywhere will rot your brain. Never has that been more apparent than now: Much of Trumpworld spent the week before an election in which they would get utterly trounced using AI to generate barely legible Anakin and Malfoid memes for an inconsequential ingroup on the social media platform run by the biggest loser on the planet.“It certainly seems like it has had its high water mark and that reality has FINALLY caught up with the Republican Party,” Michael Senters, a PhD candidate at Virginia Tech who studies online and gaming culture, told 404 Media.In 2016, 4chan posters talked about — the pseudo-ironic belief that pictures on the internet could manifest great change in reality. According to legend, Trump strategist Steve Bannon was running a gold farm when he realized the angry gamers could be harnessed into a powerful reactionary political force. Bannon and others would successfully parlay Gamergate into an that’s dominated online life in the Trump era.During the midterm livestream of Bannon’s War Room podcast, his guest read exit polls that suggested the right-wing had lost young men — a group long thought to be its strongest soldiers. The split between the parties was even, the guest explained. “That can’t be right,” , signalling he’d lost touch with the constituency he’d harnessed on behalf of Trump ten years ago. As the election results began coming in, right-wing podcasters, livestreamers, and newscasters across the internet went through at least a few of the stages of grief. First they struggled to understand what was happening, suggesting the votes must be wrong. Eventually, many of them ragequit. "Okay, I'm going to be honest. I'm absolutely rage quitting. I'm so frustrated. I am so unbelievably frustrated. I'm so mad. I think Trump didn't do 50 different things he should have done. I think he should have gone a thousand times harder. I think that he wasted his time selling trinkets and nonsense,” Asmongold said as the returns came in. He lives in Texas where Democrats swept in a shock victory.“I wish that there were more people who thought like me that weren’t sorry about it. But you know what? There’s not. So it’s just me. And that’s fine. It’s fine. It’s OK,” he said, his voice catching in his throat.Many right-wing personalities went into Tuesday somehow expecting to win despite a disastrous war, a disastrous economy, disastrous polls, and a doddering president whose closing argument seemed to be more about his ballrooms, golf courses, and the than anything else. Since Trump was re-elected, these same people have called everyone else out of touch, convinced by their X algorithm and prediction markets that no blue wave would materialize. The media has similarly spent suggesting that Bluesky is an out-of-touch while mostly failing to suggest anything of the sort about the AI-pilled Silicon Valley executives, bots, and racists shitposting on X. Tuesday’s election wipeout highlights how detached from reality the Malfoid/Anakin-shipping, X-brained billionaires and their acolytes have actually become.“Blueskywave. Those of us on here, across the board, were out of touch. I see no other conclusion,” Joe Weisenthal of Bloomberg's Odd Lots podcast (who is a serious, good journalist), said in a after the election amidst a sea of Anakins tonguing Malfoids.The meme game and general demeanor of Trump and his followers has grown wildly tiresome in his thus far-disastrous second term. Under the guidance of White House Communications Director Steven Cheung, official government accounts have , used AI to put a studio Ghibli face on anti-immigrant propaganda, and fully embraced and as cultural heroes. The base on X loved this stuff. No one else did. As our friend Gita Jackson over at Aftermath wisely put it immediately before the election, "The idea that they can meme magic their way into a red sweep by posting about Anakin Skywalker a lot is pure desperation [...] Their values have been rejected by popular culture at large, and they are now resigned to exist in the margins.”Senters said the midterms showed the hard limits of memes as a political tool. “The power that memes have has always been, in my opinion, the power to help define linguistic and community lines in the amorphous space of the Internet. You create a community when you ‘get the joke’ behind a meme but memes generally don't persuade,” he said. “I'll be curious to see if the government accounts will continue to post these far-right cultural memes in the wake of the defeat or if they'll change their tune at all. Like do they double down on the meme posting to try to rally their base? Because it very clearly had ZERO appeal to anyone outside their base.”Yet the right-wing has spent the last ten years acting as if their memes had moved the country politically. “They deluded themselves into believing that memes carry persuasive power and that their bubble on X represented material reality in a meaningful way when that was no way close to the truth,” he said. “They saw how many ‘numbers’ the Malfoid and Anakin memes did on X and convinced themselves that this was a real cultural awakening moment and that the volk were on their side.”Alyssa Mercante, an internet culture reporter who is writing a book about politics and video games called , agreed. “I think what it's really showing is that when you start to get a little bit too deep in the weeds of this hyper online culture war stuff, it cannot escape the internet,” Mercante told 404 Media. “It is not working anymore. The material reality of America is just not good enough.” Gas prices are up. Everything is more expensive. And ICE has killed Americans in the streets. “This conspiratorial mindset is wrecker mentality. It is just destructive for the sake of destruction. There is no goal beyond pulling away any sort of legitimacy from the media or from democracy,” Mercante said. “When you get so deep in the weeds of this anti-establishment conspiratorial thought process, you just can't make anything or do anything of value. You're just upending tables and pointing at them and laughing.”Democrats crushed Republicans who leaned into the online culture war during the midterms. Bo French — an who ran for railroad commissioner in Texas — to voters that depicted himself as Master Chief from Halo. His opponent beat him by more than a million votes.In Nevada, composer Martin O’Donnell ran as a Republican for a House seat and lost to incumbent Susie Lee. O’Donnell announced his campaign on Discord and leaned hard into an extremely online gamer identity. “He’s like, ‘I wrote the music and I’m voting for Trump and you should too.’ He did a LAN party campaign fundraiser. The imagery was ,” Mercante said. “This dude is like: ‘, and they're resisting this [...] and Trump is the person that is going to help us resist,’ and he's polling like absolute dog water.”It’s been 12 years since Gamergate set the tempo for online culture wars and a decade since Trump won in 2016. In 2026, Star Wars, Halo, Harry Potter feel dated in a way they didn’t back then. “What 22-year-old kid is going to be like ‘they took from me.’ They don’t know to have it taken away from them,” Mercante said. She stressed that so much right wing online culture is about distraction — she likened it to jingling keys to capture the attention of a baby. “If the economy is the number one issue for both Democrats and Republicans going into the midterms, no amount of Malfoid scissoring Anakin Skywalker is going to change that need for people to be in a better financial position,” Mercante said. “The tech oligarchs pushed this stuff straight into our eyes for two years straight unfettered [...] And I wake up and gas is this expensive? I don’t care if you take a Taylor Swift song and make JD Vance walk out to it.”“[They] really thought that this would just last forever,” she added. “When you build up a meme presidency, eventually the cards just collapse underneath you, and there's just nothing to show for it.”Though this midterm signals a move away from Gamergate-style culture war politics, both Senters and Mercante cautioned that this type of rhetoric is still dangerous, and can still be destructive. “They’re still very good at doing propaganda on the internet — they wrote the book in many cases,” Mercante said.

item.title: An AI Fraud Kingpin’s Confessions
item.author: Joseph Cox
item.content:encoded: For months I’ve been speaking to an AI fraud kingpin. You might remember in 2024 we revealed the existence of OnlyFake, an underground site that let anyone generate realistic photos of fake IDs using ‘neural networks’. The creator of that site went by the handle John Wick. A while later, the creator was arrested.Turns out there was a lot more to that story. Yuriy Nazarenko, the creator of OnlyFake, told me his side of it. How when I published my initial article he panicked, and destroyed his laptop and emails and got a new phone, paranoid that authorities were about to bust down his door. How the pressure of a growing fraud empire pushed him to drugs. And how North Korean fake IT workers used his site. Read below for his story. A few years ago, Yuriy Nazarenko sat at a desk in his grandfather’s apartment in Ukraine and, on a diet of cigarettes, Lay’s chips, and beer, painstakingly made digital copies of fake identity documents. One of his four computer screens had the messaging app Telegram open. Another displayed a scan of a passport in Photoshop filling the entire monitor.Pixel by pixel, with rap music blaring, Nazarenko edited each part of the passport. That included the MRZ codes, the block of text printed at the bottom of identity documents; the photographs to superimpose someone else’s face into the document; and the overall dimensions and quirks of each different type of passport. Nazarenko would sometimes sit for more than 12 hours at his computer, obsessively tinkering away, with a single, high-quality fake identity document taking up to a week of work.When someone thinks of fake IDs, maybe they imagine a spotty underage teen buying a physical counterfeit drivers’ license so they can score some beer. But in the global criminal underworld, digital copies or scans of IDs are like a skeleton key. A convincing scan of an ID or utility bill, loaded with a bogus name or someone else’s identity, can unlock the ability to make bank accounts, bypass checks on cryptocurrency exchanges to buy or sell more Bitcoin, or rent a safehouse, all while keeping the criminal’s real identity hidden. The digitally altered IDs need to fool both human reviewers and automated systems that scan them for inconsistencies. Making fake IDs requires exquisite attention to detail.All of that manual labor doesn’t really scale, Nazarenko thought to himself as he meticulously edited passport after passport. He went on to make templates of fake identity documents that sped up the process, but it was still slow. After many of these quiet nights, he had an idea. He built a website to automate the process that autopopulated a fake ID with the personal data a customer wanted, rather than having him do it by hand. Then, when generative AI became mainstream a short while later, he incorporated that too.“That gradually became OnlyFake,” Nazarenko told me.OnlyFake, the underground website Nazarenko made, landed like a bomb in the fraud world. It allowed anyone to generate not only convincing scans of drivers’ licenses or passports, but also realistic looking photos of those fake identity documents laying on a sofa, carpet, or desk, as if someone had taken the ID out of their wallet and snapped a picture of it on their phone. Needed a convincing looking photo of a California drivers’ license to open a cryptocurrency account in someone else’s name? Or a British passport to incorporate a company overseas? Or a Social Security card? No problem. The results were photos of identity documents that didn’t really exist, of people who may not be real, but yet could trick the sorts of people and companies that verify documents.With OnlyFake, you didn’t have to be a master forger like Nazarenko to make fake documents. Now, anyone could churn out fake IDs at scale, sometimes even hundreds or thousands at a time. OnlyFake threatened the entire idea of know-your-customer, or KYC, where financial institutions take steps to know who exactly are using its services. When anyone can make a photo of a fake ID for just a few dollars in Bitcoin, is anyone really who they say they are?Nazarenko didn’t know it then, hunched over his desk, but OnlyFake would soon become so influential that it would spawn copy cats, and the FBI would eventually arrest Nazarenko and shut down some of its competitors. The Department of Justice said in an announcement about Nazarenko’s guilty plea that OnlyFake made more than a million dollars selling fake IDs for just $15 a pop.Now for the first time, Nazarenko, 28, free after a year in prison and living in Asia, is telling his story: how North Korean fake IT workers used his creation, how he ended up in ICE detention for months after serving his sentence in the U.S., and how OnlyFake unleashed a new age of AI-powered fraud. Nazarenko said he wanted to talk to me because I was the first journalist to reveal that OnlyFake existed. This article is based on interviews with Nazarenko and his lawyer; court records; and my own reporting in the online world of fraud that OnlyFake inhabited. “OnlyFake was the first time I saw how quickly a small internet project could turn into something global. Unfortunately, it also taught me, in a very painful way, what can happen when the scale of something grows faster than your understanding of its consequences,” Nazarenko told me.Growing up, Nazarenko’s parents questioned whether Nazarenko would ever find a job. His father worked for the Security Service of Ukraine. Raised in a suburb outside of Odesa, Nazarenko jumped between a few different gigs. He worked as a cook, a waiter, at a supermarket, and as a cameraman at a local Ukrainian TV station.We continued our election coverage with a piece from Matthew Gault . There were actually a ton of proposals related to data centers on the ballot in more than 40 races across 13 states. Well, people voted against data centers in at least 38 of them. People are sick of this stuff and they’re showing up to vote about it.

item.title: Israeli Spy Company Busted Using Malware Ads To Infect, Locate, And Spy On Starlink Users
item.author: Karl Bode
item.content:encoded: Israeli spy outfit Discover-Tech spied on internet users through a sprawling network of dodgy online ads ​that it used to track, surveil, and geolocate internet users. In some instances simply having the firm’s “zero click” spyware ads displayed by devices resulted in infection. The company seemed particularly interested in using ads to surveil and geolocate Starlink users, according to a new Reuters report:“Researchers at TrendAI, a unit of Tokyo-based cybersecurity company Trend Micro (4704.T), opens new tab, ‌concluded the Israeli company Discover-Tech was one of the biggest sources of digital ads shown to users of SpaceX’s Starlink service and that the ads were likely being used to geolocate or otherwise surveil them, according to the six people.”For some reason TrendAI and Trend Micro originally didn’t formally name Discover-Tech; something only disclosed after follow up reports by both Citizen Lab and New York ad security firm Confiant. According to Citizen Lab, Discover-Tech posed as a legitimate vendor on ad exchanges, but was really just a proxy for outfits like Israel’s Candiru — a spyware company blacklisted by the U.S. government. Being broadly declared as “certified” and “approved” by unregulated establishment ad vendors and markets allowed Discover-Tech to target people with zero-click malware across more than 120,000 websites and 75,000 apps. “The totality of information gleaned from ad auctions is quite valuable. A company with access to auction data cantrack users without their knowledge as they move around in physical space, or switch between cellular, Wi-Fi, and VPNs, by observing how bid requests tied to a specific identifier change location or IP address over time. In fact, the surveillance industry sells access to so-called ad intelligence (ADINT) platforms that leverage this sort of data, often combined with third-party tracking data. In recent years, several investigations and media reports haveuncoveredvendors that sell ADINT to defense, intelligence, and law enforcement agencies.”Citizen Lab goes on to detail advancements in “zero click” ad-based malware, where simply having the ad displayed is enough to begin the infection process:“Advertisers or DSPs may run HTML and JavaScript code when an ad is shown to the user. That code retrieves additional JavaScript code, which may, in turn, load further code, such as a browser exploit to install spyware. Since the code can contain identifiers for the user or their device, arbitrary JavaScript code can be sent precisely to a single user’s device. Our research in this report indicates that this architecture is indeed abused to facilitate the delivery of zero-click targeted spyware, and that the simple display of a targeted ad is enough for infection.”Last May, Israeli newspaper reported that numerous Israeli spyware vendors had begun specifically advertising their ability to locate and spy on Starlink users, of obvious importance in military conflicts in Ukraine. We’ve noted repeatedly how the U.S. has failed to regulate data brokers and online ad markets for two primary reasons. One, the country is corrupt and repeatedly places online ad revenues above public safety, national security, and even the safety of U.S. troops. And two, the U.S. government also enjoys being able to bypass warrants by buying much of this unregulated data itself.

item.content:encoded:
NASA has unveiled the X-70 Fractal, a new crewed experimental aircraft "designed to accelerate the development and testing of advanced aviation technologies." From a press release: The crewed X-70 features advanced, rapidly reconfigurable flight-control technology that will allow NASA to explore aircraft maneuverability in ways never before demonstrated in crewed flight. The aircraft can also accommodate up to 2,000 pounds of experimental payloads in internal and external locations, enabling a wide range of research and flight-testing opportunities.
The X-70 Fractal has a takeoff weight of 10,000 pounds and is designed to cruise at Mach .75, reach altitudes of up to 45,000 feet, and provide an operational range exceeding about 1,726 miles (1,500 nautical miles). These capabilities will enable NASA to conduct demanding flight research across a broad range of operating conditions.
The X-70 joins a storied legacy of experimental aircraft that have helped establish America's leadership in aviation. From the Bell X-1, which first broke the sound barrier in 1947, to the X-15 hypersonic research aircraft and today's X-59 quiet supersonic demonstrator, NASA has spent decades pushing the boundaries of flight. With the X-70, NASA will expand its capacity to conduct experimental flight research, accelerate the testing of emerging technologies, and advance the next generation of American aviation.

item.title: Post Midterms, Pete Hegseth & RFK Jr. Stare Down Likely Impeachment Efforts
item.author: Timothy Geigner
item.content:encoded: The impact of the midterm election result is going to be felt for years, to be sure. But some of the effects will be far more swift than that, likely kicking off right after the new Congress is sworn in. We’re mere hours removed from the election, with some votes still being tallied, but already some in the media are handicapping who in the administration will remain in their positions and who will not, either because an angry Trump searching for a scapegoat fires them, or through impeachment efforts. Many people think that a third Trump impeachment will be the focus. I don’t. And I hope that’s not the route the Democrats go, though not every Techdirt writer agrees with me. I guess I’m just not all that excited to watch J.D. Vance walk into a room while Hail to the Chief plays behind him, even temporarily.I much prefer the government go after the many valid targets for impeachment that currently sit in Trump’s cabinet. And, given that both Trump and Vance are currently blaming the Iran not-a-war for the GOP loss, Pete Hegseth seems like a likely candidate to be the first to go.There are all kinds of reasons to impeach Hegseth. His injection of Christian nationalism into the DoD is plainly unconstitutional. He’s currently running a war with Iran that is without Congressional authorization has resulted in the cavalier bombing of such dastardly targets as Iranian schoolgirls. He is almost certainly personally responsible for the murder of human trafficking victims as part of his campaign to lob bombs at boats off the coast of South America because they might be running drugs. In quick order, the military under Hegseth also managed to double-tap strike its victims in these boats to ensure the victims couldn’t seek justice.Thomas Massie already has articles of impeachment for Hegseth written. But Hegseth is also an easy target for Trump to fire, which may happen before any impeachment efforts can really get kicked off. It’s not like Trump would lose much in firing Hegseth. He wasn’t qualified for the position to begin with.And neither is the other likely target of impeachment efforts: RFK Jr. The number of justifications for impeaching Kennedy are legion. He’s completely failed in his role, preferring to run podcasts and host cooking shows instead of doing his job. Measles, screwworms, pertussis are all on the rise under his failed leadership. The medical community is in full revolt over his vaccine policies. He’s hiding data from the public as to the results of his disaster of a tenure at HHS. Like Hegseth, Kennedy already has impeachment articles filed against him that are ready to go.Kennedy’s ouster from HHS is long, long overdue.None of this should be misconstrued to suggest that Democrats should take a page from Trump’s playbook and go on a revenge tour. But dismantling the corrupt, inept regime at the Secretary level makes all the sense in the world. Both Hegseth and Kennedy have been absolute disasters for the country on a variety of levels. Allowing them two more years to continue to harm the country is plainly unacceptable. And, importantly, there are Republicans that would be likely allies to impeachment efforts of both of them.The project of American restoration has to start now. Tearing down the House of MAGA must begin, brick by brick. Perhaps then, and only then, we can truly be great again.

item.title: Vietnam Jails Pirate Football Streamers For Up To a Year
item.author: BeauHD
item.content:encoded:
An anonymous reader quotes a report from TorrentFreak: A Vietnamese court has sentenced 14 people who worked on the pirate football streaming site Bun Cha TV, handing out the first prison terms we've seen since the country's piracy crackdown began earlier this year. [...] Four defendants, including the heads of the content, programming and operations teams, were sentenced to 12 months in prison. Five others received ten months, and two were sentenced to eight months. Notably, three of the site's commentators were not sent to prison. Their ten-month sentences were suspended. All 14 defendants reportedly admitted the charges and cooperated with the authorities. According to investigators, Bun Cha TV streamed more than 150,000 sports matches and it allegedly made more than 20 billion dong, roughly $760,000, in illegal profits from betting and gambling ads.
The verdict reports don't mention a total. Instead, they list illegal gains per person or team. The leader of the content team allegedly gained more than 430 million dong, while commentators made from more than 31 million to more than 480 million dong each. The verdict was picked up by Rouse, the law firm that represents the Motion Picture Association in Vietnam. In an article headlined "Strong Vietnam criminal penalties," published on Lexology on November 3, the firm calls the ruling another victory for Vietnam's IP landscape.
"The defendants were all sentenced to terms of 8-12 months in prison," Rouse writes. While Rouse is correct on the length of the terms, it doesn't mention that three of the sentences were suspended. Instead, Rouse stresses that the ruling is part of a tougher enforcement trend. "This ruling reflects a shift in enforcement strategy by Vietnamese authorities, who are increasingly moving past preliminary domain blocking to deliver criminal convictions against the operators of commercial-scale piracy rings," the firm notes. "This perhaps reflects the strength of the national crackdown following the USTR pressure in May," the firm adds. According to the indictment, Bui Ba Hien, who runs a company called S24, allegedly directed employees and collaborators to build and operate Bun Cha TV. However, Hien is not among the 14 defendants named in reports, which also do not identify the affected rightsholders.
"Interestingly, in September, Bac Ninh police issued a wanted notice for a man of the same name, Bui Ba Hien, CEO of esports company Box Vietnam," reports TorrentFreak. "This person is also charged under the same copyright statute."

item.title: DOJ Admits Its ‘Illegal Voter’ Lists Can’t Be Trusted, Leading To Three Court Losses In 24 Hours
item.author: Tim Cushing
item.content:encoded: A last minute attempt to throw the midterm election into chaos failed. Leading up to this point, the signs were never good in the Magic 8 Ball way. The Trump administration wants people to believe California was overrun with non-citizen voters. The facts, however, refuse to comply with the narrative.This particular ship has been sinking for a couple of weeks now. The DOJ delivered an accusation before it even delivered a list. It claimed — absolutely without facts in evidence — that there were 20,000 “illegal” voters in California. And by “illegal,” the administration definitely meant “brown people we’d like to expel from the country.”California pushed back. First, it questioned the claim and received no definite answer. Then the administration reluctantly admitted — as it has in other states — that its first allegation may have been overstated. But rather than pull back and reassess, the DOJ went the other way. I assure you that I am not making this next part up: it delivered a thumb drive containing a list of the 20,000 “illegal voters,” along with a password written on a Post-It note… you know, the way aging parents handle login info for their cable TV-provided email accounts. Then the state sued the DOJ, right after the DOJ demanded California investigate each and every one of these 20,000 allegations within 48 hours of being thumb-drived. Other voters sued the DOJ as well, which set it up for the string of extremely speedy failures it recently experienced. Things already looked bad for the DOJ when its DHS-aided raids in California resulted in the arrests of 28 “illegal” voters — this in a state that has 23 registered voters. Not content with this failure, the DOJ then claimed California election officials just weren’t doing enough and demanded they do all the heavy lifting while the DOJ pursued its minuscule number of prosecutions.With the mid-term election just a couple of days away, the courts moved speedily to handle this bullshit. As Chris Geidner reports, the first thing the DOJ did with the clock counting down to “FLIP EVERYTHING” time is shoot itself in the face while attempting to shoot itself in the foot:A Justice Department lawyer on Monday admitted in court that it was “fair” to say that the Trump administration’s list of “likely noncitizen” voters has a high error rate.The shocking admission from Assistant U.S. Attorney Kenneth Kao came in a hearing in a lawsuit brought last week by unions representing election workers and civil rights organizations over the Trump administration’s threatened prosecution of those election workers and other related conduct.Yep, that’s the way the DOJ does business under Trump’s control: You fuck up until you’re forced to admit you’ve fucked up. Firings and forced resignations ensue. New sychophantic rubes are pressed into service. Rinse and repeat.But what’s really enjoyable about this is how the DOJ (and the administration overseeing it) lost at of the federal court system after making this admission. Geidner has reproduced the entire timeline, which is truly a sight to behold. At 10:10 pm (ET), the federal court handling the lawsuit denied a request for a stay of its order. This led immediately to the administration running its election interference campaign to the next two levels of the court system, hoping against hope that one set of judges would give the DOJ permission to fuck with midterm elections in Calfornia. No dice. [UPDATE, 4:00 p.m. ET November 3: After a flurry of activity in the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit since Judge Thompson denied DOJ’s motion for a stay of her TRO, a 6-5 limited en banc panel of the appeals court issued an order Tuesday that stays Thompson’s TRO pending the Justice Department’s appeal of it at the Ninth Circuit.][UPDATE, 6:15 p.m. ET November 3: The plaintiffs are seeking full court en banc review at the Ninth Circuit, arguing, “Federalism principles of the highest order, embedded in our Constitution, require correction of this erroneous decision by the full Court.”]Meanwhile, the administration was trying to secure a parallel victory in the highest court in the land, pursuing its appeal of an earlier rejection of the DOJ’s lawsuit against California — one that demanded election officials “segregate” any ballots that might be related to the DOJ’s admittedly highly erroneous list of 20,000 voters.The Supreme Court couldn’t be bothered. Its rejection failed to state if it was less than impressed with the administration’s lack of subtlety when it came to its own election-rigging efforts: [ The Supreme Court quickly rejected [Solicitor General John] Sauer’s request on Monday evening — before any opposition was even sought or filed… There were no noted dissents.]So, if you’re following along and can read a clock, you’re seeing something rather remarkable: an administration being shut down by three consecutive levels of the federal court system in less than 24 hours. And that means California doesn’t have to do any of the bullshit the DOJ demanded and then sued about. It also means the DOJ doesn’t actually have any illegal election dirt on 99.9999% of California’s voters and we wouldn’t be shocked if it doesn’t have any dirt on the 28 people it managed to round up during its statewide sweep.

item.title: Congress Has Abdicated Its Role Of Holding The President In Check
item.author: Stephanie A. (Sam) Martin
item.content:encoded: But responsibility for enforcing those limits is increasingly falling to organizations, institutions and individuals outside of the legislative branch.As a scholar of the American presidency and deliberative democracy, I pay close attention to how the nation’s chief executive exercises power and communicates with the public.When presidents are allowed to break rules and disregard democratic norms without consequence, I worry that citizens will grow cynical and lose faith in the idea of self-government.As this happens, citizens may come to see the law as something that applies selectively, depending on who holds power, and lose confidence in the institutions responsible for holding their leaders accountable.They may also begin to accept the absence of accountability as a normal feature of political life, weakening the public expectations on which democratic government depends.Congress is not the only branch of government demurring from holding the president accountable.In “Trump v. United States,” the court held that former presidents cannot be criminally prosecuted for actions taken under powers the Constitution gives exclusively to the president. Along with this “absolute immunity,” the justices also granted “at least presumptive immunity” for other official acts.In their decision, the court’s conservative majority extended the meaning of official conduct to the “outer perimeter” of presidential responsibilities and prohibited courts from examining a president’s motives when determining whether an act was official.The ruling only addressed criminal liability and did not curtail Congress’ constitutional authority to investigate presidential conduct, control federal spending, enact statutory restrictions and, in serious cases, pursue impeachment.Their acquiescence is helping create a new form of official protection, which I call “practical immunity.” In using this term, I am borrowing from the work of scholars who study abuse in the American penal system.Those thinkers argue that legal obstacles, institutional hesitation and political incentives sometimes make it difficult to hold public officials accountable, even when the law suggests there has been illegal conduct.That is what appears to be increasingly happening now with Congress, the courts and the president.When Congress stops defending its lawsThe television ads case illustrates the conundrum of practical immunity.In opposing the temporary restraining order, the Trump administration’s attorneys did not contest the argument asserted by the plaintiffs – Common Cause and two unions – that the expenditures violated federal appropriations law. Instead, they said the plaintiffs lacked standing to sue. They also argued that the case was moot because the advertising campaign was ending.Those arguments failed in court. Yet the administration’s defense demonstrated how elusive enforcing a law can be when Congress fails to assert its constitutionally granted role, even when the underlying legal restriction is clear. To win, a plaintiff must establish a concrete injury and persuade a judge to intervene. While this happens, the disputed conduct often continues.The collapse of institutional rivalryThe separation of powers divides authority among the legislative, executive and judicial branches of government to prevent too much power from becoming concentrated in any one place.The architects of the Constitution anticipated that officials in different branches would compete to preserve their authority. In Federalist No. 51, James Madison argued that maintaining the balance established by the separation of powers depended on the ambitions of public officials coming into conflict. Members of Congress could be expected to resist presidential encroachments because those encroachments diminished their own power.Fierce partisanship has complicated this arrangement.Legal scholars Daryl Levinson and Richard Pildes have shown how political competition mostly now happens inside and between parties, rather than among branches of government. When one party controls Congress and the presidency, legislators may become more invested in advancing their party’s agenda than they are in defending their institution’s constitutional authority.The result is a political system in which a president can act in ways that may violate federal law, undermine democratic norms and encroach on Congress’ constitutional authority.Madison’s constitutional design assumed that public officials would defend the powers entrusted to them. The danger to the American constitutional system emerging in Trump’s second term is that congressional leaders have begun to regard those powers as expendable, allowing the president to exercise authority under conditions of practical immunity. He faces little fear of meaningful institutional consequences.

item.title: We’re Asking the Ninth Circuit to Hold Reverse Location Warrants Categorically Unconstitutional
item.author: Andrew Crocker
item.content:encoded: Yesterday, along with the ACLU, EFF filed an amicus brief in the Ninth Circuit court of appeals in United States v. Spurlock, a case involving a “tower dump” warrant. These overbroad warrants require cellular providers to turn over location data about every phone in a given area at a given time. This is the first such case to be heard by a federal appeals court since the US Supreme Court ruled this summer that highly similar “geofence” warrants are searches under the meaning of the Fourth Amendment.involves an investigation into two murder victims discovered on the side of a rural California highway. Police also found a car belonging to one of the victims several miles away on the same highway. They quickly sought a tower dump warrant for an area covering this stretch of road, which eventually revealed location data on nearly 1,700 unique phones. Faced with a motion to suppress, the district court relied on a Fifth Circuit court of appeals decision about geofence warrants to hold that tower dumps are similarly categorically unconstitutional “general warrants” that violate the Fourth Amendment. However, the court refused to suppress evidence on the basis of the “good faith doctrine.”Our amicus brief on appeal makes several key arguments.First, we point out that the Supreme Court’s decision in the geofence case this summer only strengthens the arguments that tower dumps are unconstitutional general warrants. Tower dumps are a somewhat older technique than geofence warrants, but they are both “reverse location searches,” in which police “tap into an all-encompassing database, allowing them to undertake nearly perfect, retrospective surveillance of countless persons and places.” This is the sort of untargeted “general warrant” the framers of the Fourth Amendment wanted to prevent. As we write in the brief, “Searching all people in an area without probable cause to believe they were all involved in the criminal activity under investigation reproduces the evils of general warrants and is not constitutionally permitted.” It’s this rule of law that prevents police from searching the houses of a hundred, or even a thousand people in the vicinity of a crime.Second, we note that even if high courts continue to allow tower dump and geofence warrants in any cases, core Fourth Amendment law requires strict limits to protect the privacy of innocent bystanders, including limits on the scope and duration of the warrants, as well notice to affected individuals and after-the-fact deletion and minimization of irrelevant data.Finally, we argue that the Fourth Amendment requires the court to set aside the good faith doctrine in cases like these and actually decide the constitutional issue. Too often courts pass the buck in cases involving novel surveillance techniques, leading to situations where police can continue using the technique for years or even decades without a definitive ruling.

item.title: ICE Is Now Arresting People Who’ve Been Released From ICE Detention By Court Orders
item.author: Tim Cushing
item.content:encoded: US federal court have overwhelmingly ruled (10,000 orders and counting) that migrants are — just like natural-born citizens — entitled to constitutional rights. Among them is the right to due process. This means that detained migrants have a right to a hearing to see whether they can be held in custody until a hearing on the issue. And that issue is whether or not they can be held indefinitely.The courts have said migrants have rights, far more often than not. The Trump administration has sought to counter this with an extremely novel interpretation of immigration laws that have been on the books for decades, claiming there’s ultimately no difference between someone caught crossing the border illegally (who can be detained and deported without worrying about the Constitution) and someone who has been in this country for months or years and poses no actual flight risk, much less a threat to public safety. Since it’s not on the right side of the law, the party of “law and order” has encouraged ICE to thwart the law and/or flat-out ignore court orders. ICE has made it a habit to immediately move detainees from detention center to detention center in hopes of preventing their cases from being heard. Not only does it distance migrants from their legal representation, it keeps the venue in permanent flux, which means habeas petitions are doomed to fail because they were filed in place other than where the rights violation took place (the location of the arrest). Immigrants who have been granted release from detention after winning habeas corpus petitions in court are being re-arrested by US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE).The Guardian has identified at least 20 cases nationwide relating to people who were detained after being released on habeas corpus petition in the last year, according to court records, attorneys and media reports.Twenty cases may seem like an immeasurable drop in the bucket compared to the nearly 100,000 habeas petitions that have been filed since Trump’s assault on migrants began early last year. But it’s also an obvious undercount. This determination relies on what can be gleaned from court records, which means there are likely hundreds of “re-detainees” who haven’t been able to file a motion due to ICE’s deliberate attempts to separate migrants from their rights and representation. And this effort is amazingly brutal. No normal human being would consider this to be acceptable US government behavior. But this is something the psychopaths and sociopaths running the GOP are willing to do to indulge the whims of their preferred demagogue.And in Minnesota, seven immigrants were re-detained before even exiting the Whipple federal building detention facility on the outskirts of Minneapolis, as first reported by MPR.“I don’t think being taken out of a building and directly into the arms of four or more officers complies with the court’s order,” Daniel Suitor, attorney to two of the men, said in a phone interview .In Louisiana (Fifth Circuit, yo!), immigration officials were held in contempt after re-arresting a single migrant after he’d been granted release by federal judges. More of the same is going on in Minnesota (see above) and Pennsylvania. Not only are migrants being re-arrested immediately after securing their release via court orders, but they are increasingly being deported to countries with which they have no ties. Cruelty on top of cruelty on top of hideous displays of inhumanity. That’s just the day-to-day operations of our current administration, one completely consumed by hatred and capable of little more than inflicting whatever pain it can until it runs out of time… or victims.

item.author: BeauHD
item.content:encoded:
AMD expects its fourth-quarter revenue to reach roughly $17 billion, potentially surpassing Intel's projected $15 billion to $16 billion and putting AMD ahead of its longtime rival in quarterly sales for the first time. The development reflects the companies' increasingly different positions on the market: AMD is rapidly expanding its data center CPU and AI accelerator businesses, while Intel continues to depend heavily on PC and enterprise server processors, which sales face headwinds due to high memory prices and components shortages.

item.title: American Voters Overwhelmingly Reject AI Data Centers
item.author: Matthew Gault
item.content:encoded: People across America rejected data centers during last night’s midterm election. Proposals related to data centers were explicitly on the ballot in more than 40 races across 13 states. People voted against data centers in 38 of them and counting. Six cities voted to ban data centers outright and 12 put limits on the amount of megawatts such buildings could draw. In addition to specific ballot measures, candidates who supported data centers lost across the country.One of the most striking repudiations of pro data center politicians was in Texas, where Gregg Abbott lost a bid for a fourth term as governor. Abbott had made Texas a data center friendly place. The state has more than 300 working data centers and there are plans to double that number. “Texas is the epicenter of AI development,” Abbott said in 2025 at a press conference with Google CEO Sundar Pichai. “We must ensure that America remains at the forefront of the AI revolution, and Texas is the place where that can happen.” He went on to accept more than $9 million from data center-related donors.Gina Hinojosa, Texas’s Democratic governor-elect, made Abbott’s stance on data centers a central part of her campaign. Abbott’s words about making Texas a data center-friendly AI state played on TVs and the internet over and over again. He lost by more than 700,000 votes."These midterms sent a clear message — people don't want to see data centers in their backyards,” Michael Whitesides, the deputy communications director for , told 404 Media. “Across the country, people do not see the promised benefit of these data centers, and the AI they power, playing out in their daily lives. They're seeing basic goods and services get more expensive while these billionaire backed monstrosities take up space in their community, poison their air, and drive up their utility bills.”Local Progress is a network of local elected officials. Over the past year, its members have become increasingly focused on data centers as a top political issue. “Last night, we saw local, state, and federal officials who backed data center deals lose their seats,” Whitesides said. He noted that Kim Rooney in Asheville, North Carolina and Amanda Rodrigues in San Marcos, Texas (both members of Local Progress) were elected mayors in their cities after running anti-data center campaigns.“Big Tech will continue its typical playbook of trying to buy and bully local officials into complying with their demands for more data center development, but our hope is that last night's results are a clear signal to local leaders that they can resist and their community will back them up,” Whitesides said.American voters in the communities where they’re being built They run up power bills, burn through water, and power Silicon Valley’s AI apparatus. America rejected data centers last night as both symbols of the big tech oligarchy and a physical manifestation of the future it wants to build. It’s a future Americans seem willing to fight.Elon Musk, one of the night’s big losers, took a break from a weeks-long posting spree on X as the election results rolled in. Musk spent half a billion dollars on the midterms, $224 million of it in Texas, the state where he lives and does a lot of business. The world’s richest man wanted to cover the state in data centers. Those plans aren’t looking good now that Abbott is out and Hinojoa is in.Musk broke his election day posting silence a little after 1 am. “Data centers in space looking pretty appealing right now,” on X. Chased off the land by its people, the billionaire looks to the sky.

item.title: Ofcom Admits ‘Highly Effective’ Age Checks At 16 Really Mean ‘ID Scans For Teens’
item.author: Mike Masnick
item.content:encoded: Even as the Online Safety Act was being rolled out after years of debate, UK politicians started whining and screaming that they had to follow other countries towards banning kids from social media entirely. Ofcom is supposed to help put together a plan for such a social media ban by the end of the year, with implementation set for next spring. As part of this, Ofcom was tasked with reviewing the state of technology that can determine whether someone is under or over 16, and in doing so basically confirmed what many activists have been pointing out all along: if you’re putting an explicit age limit on social media, you are requiring kids to hand over private information and put themselves at risk.The report includes this handy chart, which basically notes that if you’re trying to determine if someone is between the age of 16 and 18, you’re talking about having them hand over private information:That first column on the left is the telling one. That’s the one that says there are only four(ish) “highly effective” means of doing age assurance… and basically all of them are actually “send private info to a company.” The first two are obvious: uploading a photo ID or banking info, both of which are incredibly risky, especially since you’ll be uploading them to companies which are clear targets for hackers. The third one is really the same thing, because even as “digital identity services” are coming online with the goal of doing the ID part as a third party and then issuing some sort of “old enough” / “too young” token, those services are still getting that information via the uploading of private info.But it’s the last one that’s the funniest. For years, age verification providers have insisted that no one would have to upload private info, because they could estimate your age just based on scanning your face. But we’ve always called bullshit on that. Such scanning may be able to tell the difference between a 50-year-old and a 15-year-old but it’s effectively useless for determining the difference between a 15-year-old and a 17-year-old.And Ofcom kinda admits that. It still lists facial age estimation as “highly effective,” but only with that parenthetical caveat. And the full paper concedes that the technology falls apart for exactly the kids closest to the age line:The margin of error for facial age estimation becomes more significant for the ages closest to the target age gate (16 in this case). For example, if the facial age estimation algorithm is accurate within two years for children aged 15, it could estimate them as aged 17. This could result in significant numbers of children under 16 gaining access to services or functionalities that are restricted. It could also result in a 17-year-old being denied access if they are estimated to be 15, unless they use another method. However, this is only likely to affect users who are close to the target age, as most adults offered this method would be estimated to be clearly above 16.So, yes, if you’re much older, perhaps a facial scan gets you onto a website without uploading your ID. But if you’re anywhere near 16, you’re basically out of luck, because Ofcom’s fix for the margin of error is to kick anyone who looks young-ish over to a different method… and a different method is always going to be “upload an ID.”In order to account for the margin of error in a facial age estimation algorithm, services should implement a ‘challenge age’ (sometimes known as a ‘buffer age’). A challenge age approach is widely used in an offline context when selling age-restricted products like alcohol in retail environments, for instance, through the retailing strategy ‘Challenge 25.’ In this approach, anyone who appears to the provider of restricted products to be under the age of 25 should be challenged to provide acceptable ID proving that they are over the age of 18 if they wish to buy alcohol.Of course, requiring kids to upload their photo IDs or banking info is going to be difficult given that many kids… don’t actually have photo IDs or banking info at age 16. Ofcom argues that 89% of 16-year-olds have a passport while 19% have a provisional driving license. But passports also aren’t the kind of ID that kids regularly have at the ready any time they’re reaching an internet service. Perhaps I’m out of touch with the youth of the UK, but I’d be surprised to find many of them regularly have passports at arms length most of the time.The likely result is forcing more kids to get IDs at younger ages than they would otherwise need them, again creating privacy questions for those kids. Either way, teenagers are in for a lot of “your papers please!” and Ofcom says so pretty directly:Our preliminary assessment suggests that16- and 17-year-olds are more likely than users of other ages to need access to a photo ID document. Of the methods listed as capable of being highly effective at 16, a photo ID will likely be needed at some point in the process. This is either because the method itself requires a photo ID, because ownership of a photo ID is part of the underlying process for accessing another method (such as opening a bank account or using a digital identity service), or because a 16- or 17-year-old will most likely fall within the challenge or buffer age for facial estimation methods and be asked to prove their age with a secondary method.In other words, what UK politicians (and plenty of “child safety activists”) are demanding here is that a bunch of kids have to give up their privacy and hand over documents that can put them at risk. For their safety. At a time when there remains little to no evidence that barring kids from internet services will actually improve their safety.

item.title: Musk’s Starlink Eyes Buying Boost Mobile In Doomed Bid To Dominate Smartphones
item.author: Karl Bode
item.content:encoded: One cornerstone of Elon Musk’s fraud-packed SpaceX IPO prospectus includes the claim that they’ll extremely quickly (as in a year or two) boost Starlink subscriber totals from 13 million to something closer to 300 million. Given the network’s congestion problems and physics constraints, that’s simply not realistic. Also: more users means even greater capacity problems and weird network restrictions.To try and goose growth, Starlink has recently been making it clear they’d like to try and get into the cellular and smartphone business. But the actual plan is, as with all things Musk, a misleading, hot mess.A key part of Starlink’s plan includes plunking down thousands of meshed femtocells installed on customer rooftops alongside existing LEO satellite dishes, something one telecom analyst recently stated was “one of the top three dumbest ideas in my four decades of being in this industry.” In part because the femtocell installations are just logistically annoying and complicated, and will further will eat up capacity on the increasingly congested network (recall that Starlink customers in some areas already face “congestion fees” as high as $1500).“SpaceX has held talks with telecom firm EchoStar in recent months about launching its own signature wireless service through a deal with the company, the report said, citing ​people familiar with the negotiations. The move would support the Elon Musk-led ​company’s plans to build a hybrid satellite-terrestrial mobile network through Starlink ⁠Mobile, combining its satellite constellation with ground-based infrastructure to challenge US wireless ​giants AT&T, Verizon and T-Mobile.”One problem? Boost mobile is just a mobile virtual network operator (MVNO). It’s primarily just customer-facing retail artifice that runs on the back of existing AT&T and T-Mobile networks; neither of which is keen to have their cozy regional telecom dominance disrupted. To actually compete, Musk and Starlink would still need to invest hundreds of billions of additional dollars in a high-powered 5G network over the next decade. And even then there’s no guarantee of success.You might recall that Boost Mobile was offloaded to Echostar as part of that doomed first-term Trump administration effort to approve the Sprint-T-Mobile merger, then hide its labor and competition impact by pretending that Dish Network would build a successful replacement 5G network. That of course never happened; the real impact was mass layoffs, higher prices and worse service for everybody. Regardless: U.S. telecom is just generally a shitty market to try and disrupt. It’s extremely expensive and time consuming, and at every turn you’re likely to get creatively ratfucked by giants like AT&T and Verizon, whose political influence over Republicans historically rivals Musk’s. Again, even traditionally staid and bullish telecom trade mags have expressed concerns that Starlink’s smartphone push is doomed. I think this mostly all exists as a way for Starlink to hoard valuable spectrum and goose stock valuations. There may be some people at Starlink who have convinced themselves this will actually work (the fact SpaceX has been lobbying for phone unlocking rules suggests some potential earnestness), but U.S. telecom history is littered with these sorts of half-assed disruption efforts that routinely go nowhere. I’m not prone to believe things that come out of the mouths of Verizon executives, but in this case I think Verizon CEO Dan Schulman is correct when he states it would cost SpaceX something akin to $300-$500 billion and five years build a network capable of really competing with cellular giants. And that’s just network infrastructure; you still need to convince users to sign up, provide a quality experience, and provide useful customer support (something Musk companies historically aren’t interested in). While fending off the political machinations of AT&T, Verizon, and T-Mobile, who all but own the legislature in most states after a generation of lobbying and campaign contribution. The Musk cult and our shitty corporate press will spend the next few years enamored with the fiction that “Musk is disrupting smartphones,” but this mostly just reads as further stock-fluffing performance by a man with more money than sense.
